title: Raga Todi
hook: a morning raga that opens by admitting need

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Jaitsri: whole at the beginning, whole in the middle, whole at the end. Your line was strength in jaitsri. What middle did you give an unhurried minute? Day one thousand eighty-eight.

The first minutes after waking are strange ones. The armor isn't on yet. Before the to-do list and the phone and the public face, there's a softer person blinking at the ceiling, who might, for a moment, say what they actually need. Tradition calls today's raga a morning raga, and a tender one. And the hymn that opens it sounds exactly like that unguarded first minute: no ceremony, no long praise, just an honest sentence about need. Today: Raga Todi, and a morning without armor.
screen: `THE FIRST MINUTES AFTER WAKING.` → `BEFORE THE ARMOR GOES ON.` → `AN HONEST SENTENCE ABOUT NEED.`

segments.voice: Todi comes after Jaitsri in the Granth's order. Its first hymn is by Guru Ram Das, mahala four. It begins: har bin reh na sakai man mera. In paraphrase: without the Lord, my mind cannot live. No argument, no description of God's greatness, just a statement of dependence, the way a child says I need you. That line opens the refrain, the rahao, the part the hymn keeps coming back to, and the refrain goes on, in paraphrase: my beloved, the breath of my life, is the Lord; the Guru has brought me to meet him, and I won't be tossed again on the terrifying ocean of the world. Notice the order. First the need, said plainly. Then the beloved, named as breath, as close as the air going in and out. Then the meeting, and the steadiness that follows. That's what tender means here. Not weak, not sentimental. Tender is what a person sounds like when they stop pretending to be self-sufficient. A tender morning is a morning that starts by telling the truth about what it can't live without. Tradition sets Todi in the morning, and teachers describe the moods of ragas in different ways, so hold the hour lightly. But you can hear why the Guru's opening words would sit well at dawn, before the armor goes on. Today's line: tender morning.
screen: `TODI FOLLOWS JAITSRI.` · `WITHOUT THE LORD, MY MIND CANNOT LIVE.` · `THE BELOVED, THE BREATH OF MY LIFE.` · `TENDER: NO LONGER PRETENDING.` · then, large: `TENDER MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Todi, and take the armor off for a minute. If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Todi; a morning recording is a good choice. Then sit. Let the shoulders drop. Unclench the jaw. Let the hands open, palms up, on your knees. Breathe as if you'd just woken. Then, quietly, finish this sentence for yourself: without this, I couldn't live. A person, a faith, the breath itself. Don't explain it. Just let it be true for a while. If you pray, you can let the answer be Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Raga Todi. The short section after Jaitsri, a morning raga in tradition, which opens with Guru Ram Das saying: without the Lord, my mind cannot live. Today's word.
Your line: tender morning. Tomorrow, in the first minute after waking, before you touch your phone, say one honest sentence about what you need. Day one thousand eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Shabads from the Todi section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Todi in kirtan, including in morning programs at some gurdwaras, following the tradition that links Todi with the morning.
